title: Crawler Blast-Hole Drill Rig (89–127 mm)
model_title: Crawler Blast-Hole Drill Rig (top-hammer / DTH, 89–127 mm holes)

introduction.definition: The crawler blast-hole drill rig drills the holes that are charged with explosives to break the hard ferricrete caprock (and occasional hard ore). The rig trams to each pegged hole, levels itself, sets the boom and tilts the feed forward from the tramming position to the design angle, then pushes the feed foot onto the ground. The hydraulic rock drill hammers and rotates the drill rods while compressed air from the on-board screw compressor flushes the cuttings out of the hole; the collar hood and dust collector capture the fines. Hole depth covers the caprock plus a short sub-drill.
applications: Production drilling of caprock / hard ore for blasting
Secondary drilling of oversize boulders (where not broken by the rock breaker), and occasional hard ore lenses
Grade-control sampling is done by a separate RC rig (01-RC)
key_points: Holes 89–127 mm on a ~3.0 × 3.5 m pattern (burden × spacing) in caprock 0.5–3 m thick; where the caprock is thinner than ~1–1.5 m, rip it with a dozer instead
Top hammer: percussion + rotation at the shank; DTH: hammer at the bit (larger holes)
Flushing air goes down the hollow rods and carries the cuttings up the annulus; the collar hood and dust collector protect people and the environment
Accurate collar position and depth from GNSS high-precision guidance
Log every hole (depth, water, voids, caprock/ore contact); the shotfirer charges to the log
Never drill into or near an old socket/butt or a misfired hole
Holes are dipped, charged with bulk emulsion (always in wet holes) or ANFO (dry holes only) and stemmed under the blast plan
Short holes: stemming ~2 m (≈ 17–25 × hole diameter) of crushed aggregate leaves only ~1 m of charge; too little stemming causes flyrock and cratering — follow the blast design and the hole log

classification.type: Crawler surface drill rig, top-hammer/DTH, 89–127 mm

introduction.summary: A self-propelled crawler drill rig drills the blast holes that break the hard ferricrete caprock (and any hard ore). The feed (mast) is raised to vertical, the hydraulic rock drill (top hammer — or a down-the-hole hammer on larger rigs) hammers and rotates the drill string into the rock while the screw compressor blows flushing air down the rods that carries the cuttings up to the collar hood and dust collector. Holes of 89–127 mm on a ~3.0 × 3.5 m pattern are then charged with bulk emulsion/ANFO.

interfaces: Drills ahead of 01-EX loading after 01-DZ stripping
Blast charged by the explosives MMU (contractor)

what_to_look_for: The hole goes through the caprock and about 0.3–0.5 m of sub-drill into the soft ore, so the charge breaks the full caprock without a hard toe.
After charging, the upper ~2 m of each hole is stemming (crushed aggregate) and the ~1 m charge column of emulsion sits in the lower caprock and sub-drill — see the far hole on the section.

steps.text: The rig trams to the pegged hole with the feed in the tramming position, checks the collar for old sockets or misfire signs, and levels on its tracks.

The boom places the feed over the hole; the feed is tilted forward from the tramming position to the design angle (here vertical) and the feed foot is pressed onto the ground. The centraliser at the foot guides the rods while collaring.
The rock drill delivers rapid percussion blows (~40–60 Hz) and rotation through the rod to the button bit; the feed force keeps the bit in contact.

Flushing air from the screw compressor passes through the rock drill and down the hollow rods, leaves at the bit face and carries the cuttings up the annulus to the collar hood; the dust collector sucks off and filters the fines.
The hole goes through the caprock and about 0.3–0.5 m of sub-drill into the soft ore, so the charge breaks the full caprock without a hard toe.
After charging, the upper ~2 m of each hole is stemming (crushed aggregate) and the ~1 m charge column of emulsion sits in the lower caprock and sub-drill — see the far hole on the section.
At design depth the string is withdrawn while flushing, the feed foot is lifted, the feed is put in the tramming position and the rig trams to the next hole.

working_principle.characteristic_curve: Penetration rate falls as rock strength (UCS) rises and as the bit wears; regrinding the buttons restores it.

commissioning: Feed alignment and hole-angle calibration; GNSS navigation calibration; dust collector and fire-suppression checks; rod-handling interlocks; anti-jamming test.

routine.task: Walk-around: rods, bit, shank, hoses and whip checks, dust-collector filters, tracks.
Regrind the bit buttons before the wear flat reaches ~1/3 of the button diameter, or at the first sign of snakeskin/micro-cracks (typically every 20–80 m in abrasive caprock; track per bit).
Grease the threads at every rod/bit change; replace the shank adapter by wear/striking-face inspection.

periodic.task: Check the rock-drill accumulator gas pre-charge.
Compressor and engine service; air-filter change.

overhaul.task: Feed slides, chains/cylinder and cradle wear parts.

lubrication: Shank lubrication (air-oil) during drilling; grease feed, cradle and carousel; compressor oil to schedule.

symptoms: Explosive residue or a socket at the collar
causes: Butts not marked after the last blast
remedies: Stop, do not withdraw the rods, evacuate, call the shotfirer; post-blast inspection marks all butts

symptoms: Rotation pressure rises, string will not retract
remedies: Increase flushing, reduce feed force, back-hammer; avoid drilling through voids

symptoms: Hole cannot be dipped to design depth
Cuttings fall back when the string is withdrawn
causes: Clay-rich or broken caprock, poor flushing, rain
remedies: Clean out by redrilling; use hole liners/collar pipes or stemming plugs; log and flag for the shotfirer
Log the water depth; charge with emulsion (water-resistant), not ANFO; dewater holes and plan to blast quickly

causes: Feed misalignment, excessive feed force, fast collaring
remedies: Recalibrate the feed; collar gently; correct the feed force

causes: Dust-collector filter blocked, hood not seated
remedies: Clean/replace filters; seat the hood; water injection

safety: Never drill into or within the site minimum distance of an old socket/butt, a bootleg or a misfired hole; inspect and mark the pattern before drilling and report any suspected explosive residue to the shotfirer.
Never drill in a pattern once charging has started, except under the site procedure and at the site minimum distance from charged holes.
Check overhead clearance before raising or tramming with the feed up: the ~9 m mast must keep the site minimum approach distance to power lines.
Position the rig at right angles to the crest and outside the edge-hazard zone (site rule) when drilling the front row; tram with the feed in the tramming position, within OEM slope/tilt limits.
Rotating rods and rod handling: exclusion zone around the feed while drilling, guards and rod-handling interlocks, never reach into the feed.
Respirable crystalline silica and noise (top hammer > 100 dB(A) at the rig): dust collector working, closed pressurised cab, RPE and hearing protection outside the cab.
Before maintenance: isolate, blow down the compressor and air lines (whip checks on hoses), and depressurise the hydraulics and rock-drill accumulators (LOTO).
After charging: blast exclusion zone as the site blast plan sets (typically ≥ 300–500 m for people and ≥ 100–200 m for equipment, machines facing away) and misfire procedures.
Lightning warning (detector or site alert): stop charging, clear the blast area and the charged pattern to the exclusion distance.
Whip checks on all air couplings; depressurise before breaking a connection.

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Crawler Blast-Hole Drill Rig (89–127 mm).
Walk-around: rods, bit, shank, hoses and whip checks, dust-collector filters, tracks.
Regrind the bit buttons before the wear flat reaches ~1/3 of the button diameter, or at the first sign of snakeskin/micro-cracks (typically every 20–80 m in abrasive caprock; track per bit).
Grease the threads at every rod/bit change; replace the shank adapter by wear/striking-face inspection.
Check the rock-drill accumulator gas pre-charge.
Rock-drill service/reseal.
Rock-drill overhaul.
Feed slides, chains/cylinder and cradle wear parts.
Watch for drilling into a misfire / butt: explosive residue or a socket at the collar. Common cause: butts not marked after the last blast.
Watch for stuck rods: rotation pressure rises, string will not retract. Common cause: broken ground, poor flushing.
Watch for hole collapse / blocked hole: hole cannot be dipped to design depth. Common cause: clay-rich or broken caprock, poor flushing, rain.
Record every inspection so trends — wear, temperatures, pressures, leaks and performance — can be compared over time.

questions.question: What does the flushing air do?
options: Cools the cab
Lifts cuttings out of the hole and cools the bit
Drives the tracks
Charges the hole with explosive
questions.explanation: Air goes down the hollow rods, out of the bit and back up the annulus carrying the cuttings.

questions.question: In a top-hammer rig, where is the hammer?
options: On the compressor
On the feed carriage at the top of the rods
At the bit in the hole
In the cab
questions.explanation: DTH hammers sit at the bit; top hammers ride the feed.

questions.question: Why is a short sub-drill added below the caprock?
options: To sample ore
To anchor the rig
So the blast breaks the full caprock thickness without leaving a hard toe
To reach groundwater
questions.explanation: A short sub-drill (~0.3–0.5 m) lets the charge break the full caprock without a hard toe; going deeper into soft ore wastes energy and dilutes ore.

questions.question: What sets the burden and spacing?
options: The rod length
The blast design (hole diameter, bench height, rock strength, fragmentation target)
The truck payload
The rig's tramming speed
questions.explanation: Pattern geometry and powder factor come from the blast design.

questions.question: Who charges the holes with explosives?
options: The drill operator alone
A trained charging crew under the licensed shotfirer, to the blast plan
Any operator
Truck drivers
questions.explanation: Explosives handling is licensed and controlled; the shotfirer is responsible.

questions.question: You find an old socket near a pegged hole. What do you do?
options: Do not drill; mark it and report to the shotfirer/supervisor
Drill through it quickly
Flush it with air
Move the peg 0.5 m and drill
questions.explanation: An old socket can hold undetonated explosive; drilling into or near it can set it off.

pre_start: Walk-around, check rods and bit, hoses and whip checks, dust collector, fluid levels, fire suppression
start_up: Warm up the engine and hydraulics, then load the compressor; test feed movement, anti-jamming and interlocks
normal: Check the collar for old sockets/misfire indications before collaring
Navigate to the hole, level, set the boom, raise the feed, push the foot down, collar gently, drill to depth with steady feed and flushing
Withdraw while flushing; record depth, penetration, water, voids and the caprock/ore contact
shut_down: Withdraw the string while flushing, feed to tramming/transport position
Park on level ground away from the crest and outside any charged area
Unload the compressor and let it blow down, cool down the engine, engine off, isolate

Flushing-air pressure low/high (blocked bit or collapse)
Rod-handling and feed guard interlocks; cab-door/E-stop interlock on feed and percussion
tips: Collar slowly to avoid hole deviation
Report broken or wet ground to the blast engineer
